title: Chapter 2 — Heat
paragraphs: What happens when heat enters a cool town? The chapter opens with Ta, Goy's brother, home from the army — odd, unpredictable, "a bit ting-tong" after opium years in Chiang Mai. Nobody confronts him and nobody laments; Mae Daeng absorbs him into the household and stays cool. When he drops a wardrobe and walks out, Goy shrugs.

Then the heat finds Julia. Without explanation Mae Daeng asks her to leave the house; days later, after a dream, she is invited back — and the rupture is never spoken of again. Gaew coaches her through it: don't keep the feeling at all. When Julia snaps at an aunt over an English lesson, the reprimand lands hard. Learning fieldwork, she realizes, means learning to laugh first, smile second, and eventually not to feel the flash at all.

The control case arrives on holiday: Laina, an American twenty-year-old, argues with Julia over dinner the way Americans argue — and Gaew and Aung are visibly alarmed. What reads as ordinary disagreement in one register reads as a fight in the other. Even visiting toddler Kuni, exuberant and loud, draws the grandmotherly verdict from Mae Lah: "a bit too... American."

Needing a comparison community, Julia follows Gaew's suggestion ten kilometers up a dirt road to Ban Ko Tao, a S'gaw Karen village that has been Baptist for a century. Duansri — farmer, weaver, mother of Min and May, one of fifteen siblings — takes her in. Her cousin Jerapong, the widely traveled pastor, is the village's center of gravity; his wife Sada keeps the trilingual Bible; his uncle Paw Pu, pastor before him, presides from the porch; her husband P'Duang, a buffalo-trading Northern Thai, is the village's one Buddhist.

Church is warm where the wat is cool: singing, testimony, weeping, enthusiasm. When a Kansas missionary preaches fire and brimstone, Jerapong renders it gently into Karen and confides afterward, "I didn't translate that part." Karen interviewees say feelings should be spoken; Mae Jaeng interviewees say they should be cooled. Each side keeps a stereotype of the other.

The chapter ends at the university, where Ajarn Somwang confirms what the fieldwork kept implying: Thai has no word for "emotion." There are feelings, moods, and above all the jai — the heart — with its hundreds of compounds. When Julia is upset, Chai asks not "how do you feel?" but "gone yet?" Emotion, in Mae Jaeng, is weather: it is not processed; it passes.
